headline: High-risk shared-workspace and MCP pathways: Continue can write and egress by default while awesome-prompts is a prompt source, creating injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt/content source, and Continue can ingest workspace files and MCP outputs; if prompt text from A is copied into B or exposed through a shared workspace/MCP channel, B may treat attacker-controlled instructions as trusted content. The pairwise bridge is plausible but not directly documented, so I choose medium over low due to uncertainty escalation.
conditions: IF content from agent_a is copied into agent_b's workspace or MCP-fed context
IF agent_b parses file or MCP content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable MCP servers for the session
Keep agent_a content in a separate, read-only folder
Require explicit provenance labels on pasted prompt text
Review any prompt files before opening them in agent_b

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b reads and writes workspace files and can send context to user-chosen model providers or MCP servers; agent_a is a prompt repository that may contain sensitive pasted material if reused operationally. Because B has broad egress and file access while A is a content source, shared-workspace leakage is plausible in default use, though not proven from direct interaction evidence.
conditions: IF sensitive prompts or secrets are stored in files derived from agent_a
IF agent_b is configured to send workspace context to a third-party model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Store sensitive prompts outside the shared workspace
Use a local-only model provider in agent_b
Audit MCP server endpoints before enabling them
Remove secrets from any prompt templates before opening them

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b has write_filesystem, execute_shell, install_packages, and broad network egress, while agent_a is a content-writing source with no runtime controls. If both operate on the same directory, B can overwrite or consume A-derived files and create conflicting edits; the shared-state-via-filesystem model makes this a default-pathway concern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem path
IF agent_b writes files that agent_a or downstream tooling also reads
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Make agent_a outputs read-only
Use per-task subfolders for B
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can act on workspace content and tool outputs, while awesome-prompts supplies prompt material that may be treated as authoritative by a user or downstream workflow. If A-derived instructions are fed into B without verification, B can propagate or operationalize errors; the interaction is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as task instructions or source material
IF no human verification step occurs before B acts on A-derived content
mitigations: Add a verification step before execution
Mark A-derived text as untrusted input
Require human approval for any action based on prompt content
Separate drafting from execution roles

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or certification mismatch is documented for agent_a, and agent_b only explicitly handles source code, open editor buffers, and model-provider API keys. The pair does not show a concrete compliance breach pathway from the profiles alone, so only a low residual gap remains; the other agent is cited because the assessment is pairwise.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is placed into agent_b buffers
IF the configured model provider or MCP server has stricter residency or retention rules than the workspace
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace
Use a provider with documented residency controls
Review retention settings before enabling sync
Avoid storing secrets in editor buffers
